related_questions.question: Can fingernails show signs of illness?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, fingernails can show signs of various illnesses. Changes in nail color, shape, or texture can sometimes indicate underlying health conditions ranging from nutritional deficiencies to more serious diseases.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, fingernails can show signs of various illnesses

list.snippet: Pale nails: May suggest anemia or congestive heart failure.
Half-and-half nails (half pink, half white): Can be a sign of kidney disease.
Yellow nails: May indicate a fungal infection, lung disease, or in rare cases, thyroid issues or diabetes.
Blue nails: Can signal low oxygen levels in the blood, potentially due to lung or heart conditions.
White nails (Terry's nails): Can be associated with liver problems, congestive heart failure, or diabetes.
Clubbed nails (bulging fingertips with nails curving around them): May indicate lung or heart problems, inflammatory bowel disease, or HIV/AIDS.
Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails): Can be a sign of iron deficiency anemia or lupus.
Pitted nails: Pits or dents in the nails can be associated with psoriasis or alopecia areata.
Dark lines or spots under the nail: While often due to injury or moles, they can sometimes indicate melanoma (a type of skin cancer).
Horizontal lines (Beau's lines): Can be a sign of recent illness, injury, or malnutrition.
Brittle, peeling nails: May be related to nutritional deficiencies, thyroid issues, or frequent hand washing.
Splinter hemorrhages (small red or brown lines under the nails): Can indicate a heart valve infection or other conditions.
Separation of the nail from the nail bed (onycholysis): May be linked to psoriasis, fungal infections, or thyroid problems.
Not all nail changes indicate serious illness. Many changes can be caused by injury, age, or lifestyle factors.
A single nail abnormality is rarely cause for alarm, but if you notice persistent or concerning changes, it's best to consult with a doctor or dermatologist.
Early detection of nail problems can sometimes help identify underlying medical conditions and facilitate timely treatment.

related_questions.question: What nails can tell you about your health?

text_blocks.snippet: Changes in nail appearance, such as color, shape, or texture, can sometimes indicate underlying health issues. While not all nail changes are cause for alarm, some can signal vitamin deficiencies, infections, or even more serious conditions like heart, lung, or liver problems.
snippet_highlighted_words: Changes in nail appearance, such as color, shape, or texture, can sometimes indicate underlying health issues

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at what your nails might be telling you:

list.snippet: Pale nails: May indicate anemia, congestive heart failure, or liver disease.
Yellow nails: Can suggest a fungal infection, lung disease, or even diabetes.
Blue nails: May be a sign of low oxygen levels in the blood, possibly related to heart or lung conditions.
White spots or streaks (leukonychia): While often harmless, they can sometimes indicate zinc deficiency or other conditions.
Dark lines or streaks (melanonychia): Can be a sign of melanoma (skin cancer), but also a normal variant in darker skin tones.
Clubbing (swollen, rounded fingertips): May signal lung or heart disease, liver cirrhosis, or gastrointestinal issues.
Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia): Can indicate iron deficiency anemia.
Pitting (small dents in the nail surface): May be associated with psoriasis, alopecia areata, or eczema.
Beau's lines (horizontal grooves): Can be caused by recent illness, stress, or injury.
Brittle or splitting nails: May be due to vitamin deficiencies, thyroid problems, or even drug use.
Thickened nails: Can be a sign of fungal infection or psoriasis.
Separation from the nail bed (onycholysis): May be caused by injury, infection, or psoriasis.
Peeling skin around the nails: Can be a sign of fungal infection, psoriasis, or eczema.
Ingrown nails: Can be painful and may require medical attention, especially if they become infected.
Red or brown streaks: May be splinter hemorrhages (small blood vessel ruptures) or, in some cases, a sign of skin cancer.
Ragged or crumbly nails: Can be a sign of nutritional deficiencies or other health problems.
Any unusual or persistent changes in your nails should be evaluated by a healthcare professional, says Dr. Poblete-Lopez at Cleveland Clinic.
Early diagnosis and treatment can be crucial for managing underlying health conditions.
If you notice any concerning nail changes, such as severe discoloration, pain, or swelling, consult a doctor promptly.

text_blocks.snippet: In many cases, nail changes are harmless and can be attributed to age, injury, or minor infections. However, it's always best to err on the side of caution and seek professional advice when you have any doubts or concerns about your nail health.

related_questions.question: How to identify disease from nails?

text_blocks.snippet: Nail changes, such as discoloration, shape alterations, or texture irregularities, can be indicators of underlying systemic diseases. For example, pale nails can suggest anemia, while bluish nails might indicate a lack of oxygen due to lung or heart issues. Changes in nail shape, like spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), can be associated with iron deficiency anemia or hemochromatosis. Other changes, such as pitting, splinter hemorrhages, or clubbing, may also be linked to various conditions like psoriasis, bacterial endocarditis, or lung disease.
snippet_highlighted_words: Nail changes, such as discoloration, shape alterations, or texture irregularities

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at how to identify potential nail diseases:

list.snippet: Pale nails: Can indicate anemia, liver or kidney disease, or poor nutrition.
Bluish nails: May suggest a lack of oxygen, potentially due to lung or heart problems.
Yellow nails: Can be caused by fungal infections, lung or thyroid problems, or smoking.
White nails with a pink band at the tip (Terry's nails): May indicate liver or kidney disease.
White spots or lines: Can be caused by injuries, zinc deficiency, or fungal infections.
Dark lines (longitudinal melanonychia): Can be normal, but may also be a sign of melanoma, especially if they are new or changing.
Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails): May be a sign of iron deficiency anemia or hemochromatosis.
Clubbing (widening and rounding of the fingertips and nails): Can be associated with lung disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or heart disease.
Onycholysis (separation of the nail from the nail bed): May indicate hyperthyroidism or psoriasis.
Beau's lines (horizontal ridges): Can be caused by illness, injury, or exposure to cold temperatures.
Pitting: Small dents or depressions in the nail plate, often associated with psoriasis or eczema.
Brittle nails: Can be caused by aging, thyroid issues, or nutritional deficiencies.
Thickening of the nails: May indicate fungal infections, psoriasis, or other conditions.
Thinning or crumbling nails: Can be a sign of nutritional deficiencies, thyroid problems, or certain medications.
Splinter hemorrhages (small lines of blood under the nail): Can be caused by bacterial endocarditis, trauma, or other conditions.
Swelling, redness, or pain around the nails: May indicate infection (paronychia), injury, or other inflammatory conditions.
Nail separation from the nail bed: Can be a sign of injury, infection, or other conditions.

text_blocks.snippet: It is important to consult with a healthcare provider if you notice any significant or persistent changes in your nails, especially if they are accompanied by other symptoms. Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent nail problems from worsening and impacting overall health.

text_blocks.snippet: Nail symptoms can range from minor cosmetic changes to signs of underlying health conditions. Common symptoms include changes in nail color, shape, and thickness, as well as pain, swelling, or separation from the nail bed. These changes can be caused by infections, injuries, or systemic diseases.
snippet_highlighted_words: changes in nail color, shape, and thickness, as well as pain, swelling, or separation from the nail bed

list.title: Color Changes:
list.snippet: Pale, yellow, white (including white spots or leukonychia), dark streaks (melanonychia), or red or brown streaks can indicate various conditions, including anemia, kidney disease, lung disease, or infections.

list.title: Shape Changes:
list.snippet: Nail clubbing (rounded, bulging nails), spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), or nails that curve abnormally can be associated with heart, lung, or liver conditions.

list.title: Texture Changes:
list.snippet: Brittle, thin, or crumbly nails can result from frequent wetting and drying, chemical exposure, or underlying conditions like iron deficiency.

list.title: Thickness Changes:
list.snippet: Thickened nails can be a sign of fungal infections or other conditions.

list.title: Nail Separation:
list.snippet: Onycholysis, where the nail separates from the nail bed, can be caused by psoriasis, infections, or thyroid issues.

list.title: Pitting:
list.snippet: Small dents or depressions in the nail surface can be associated with psoriasis, eczema, or alopecia areata.

list.title: Pain, Swelling, or Redness:
list.snippet: These symptoms around the nail can indicate paronychia (nail infection) or other inflammatory conditions.

list.title: Ridges:
list.snippet: Vertical ridges are common with aging, but horizontal ridges (Beau's lines) can signal underlying illnesses.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to see a doctor if you experience any persistent or concerning nail changes, especially if accompanied by other symptoms. Nail problems can be a clue to various health issues, and early diagnosis and treatment can be crucial, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.
